title: The top of the pole
hookLine: how do you step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole? (Gateless Gate 46)

lines: TEETH, A NAME, FLAX, A TREE.
cards: This week opened with Dogen telling us how to sit, then saying the blue mountains walk. Then the koans, one a day: a man hanging by his teeth, a monk calling his own name, three pounds of flax, a cypress tree.

Each took away somewhere to stand: no safe answer, no faraway meaning. Today's case goes all the way up. A teacher named Shishuang asks: from the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you take one step forward?

teach.b: First, the picture. A pole a hundred feet high, and someone who has climbed it all the way. Every hand over hand was real work.
Now they're balanced at the top, sky all around, and Shishuang doesn't ask how you got here. He asks how you step forward from here, with no more pole to climb. Second, an older warning.
The case adds the words of a teacher from long before. In paraphrase: someone sitting on top of the pole has got somewhere, but it isn't yet the real thing.

teach.h: ONE MORE STEP, IN ALL DIRECTIONS.
teach.b: They need one more step, showing their whole body in all ten directions.

teach.h: THE TOP CAN BE A TRAP.
teach.b: Third, why the top can be a trap. Some teachers read the top as an attainment you can hold onto: a calm you finally reached, a breakthrough in sitting, a self-image as someone who gets it.
It feels like arriving, and the case says arriving is where you get stuck. Stepping off doesn't mean throwing practice away.
Some readers hear it as letting go of the height itself and coming back down into the whole world, ordinary life included. Fourth, the week.

teach.h: THE FLAX, THE TREE, THE POLE.
teach.b: The flax and the cypress said: it's right here.
The pole says it from the other side. Even what you reached by climbing becomes a new place to cling. The koan asks for one more step, and leaves the stepping to you.

how: In Rinzai Zen this case is given as a koan, and teachers sometimes use the image of the pole's top to warn students against holding on to a calm or insight they have reached in sitting.

games.q: what does “the top of the pole” mean?
o: a height reached in practice that can become a trap
a test of courage for monks in old Chan temples
the highest stage of awakening, where practice ends

games.q: the top of the pole: tap the pairs.
p: your whole body in ten directions

s: the case praises whoever reaches the top of the pole
it says they've got somewhere, but it isn't yet the real thing.
the old teacher in the case says to show the whole body in all ten directions
one more step, and the whole body appears everywhere.
stepping off the pole means quitting practice
some readers hear it as letting go of the height and coming back into the whole world.

games.q: you've climbed a hundred-foot pole. you're at the top, balanced and calm. Shishuang asks how you'll step forward. what does the case point toward?
o: climb back down the way you came.
take one more step, into all ten directions.
games.why: the old teacher in the case says sitting on top isn't yet the real thing; take one more step and show the whole body in the ten directions.

practice: Think of one place you've climbed to and now hold tightly, a routine, a way of being seen, a comfort you guard, and notice without judging how your body holds it, in the shoulders or the jaw.
Then, on an out-breath, picture loosening that grip by a single degree: one small step past comfort, not a leap. Rest there.

wordCard.voice: The top of the pole. Shishuang's question in case forty-six of the Gateless Gate: from the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you step forward? Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: 'the top of a hundred-foot pole'. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

carryVoice: Your line: step off the pole. Even the top is a place to let go of. That's the week.
